title: Research Bite #72: The Effects of School Phone Bans: National Evidence from Lockable Pouches
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #72 covers Hunt Allcott, E. Jason Baron, Thomas Dee, Angela Duckworth, Matthew Gentzkow, and Brian A. Jacob's 'The Effects of School Phone Bans: National Evidence from Lockable Pouches,' an NBER working paper (No. 35132, 2026) also released via SSRN and Stanford SIEPR. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design across Yondr-adopting schools nationwide (roughly 1,341 middle schools and 656 high schools in the test-score analysis, plus a ~108,000-response national teacher survey), the researchers combined GPS phone-signal data, standardized test scores, attendance, discipline records, and student surveys to evaluate lockable phone pouches. The intervention worked as intended at cutting phone use -- teacher-reported in-class personal phone use fell from 61% to 13% -- but the downstream effects were surprisingly modest and mixed. Disciplinary incidents actually rose and student well-being dipped in the first year of adoption (a short-term disruption effect), before well-being turned positive and discipline effects faded in later years. Average test scores barely moved overall, with small high-school maths gains offset by small middle-school declines, and there was little evidence of effects on attendance or bullying.
points: The finding that phone bans sharply reduce phone use (61% to 13%) but produce only modest, mixed downstream effects on achievement and well-being is a direct challenge to the assumption that cutting phone access alone will meaningfully move academic or behavioral outcomes.

The first-year dip in well-being and rise in disciplinary incidents -- followed by recovery in later years -- suggests schools implementing pouch bans should expect a genuine adjustment period, not immediate gains, and should not abandon the policy based on early results alone.

The split effect on test scores (small high-school maths gains, small middle-school dips) means a blanket 'phone bans help/don't help academics' claim is too coarse; the effect appears to interact with school level.
Near-zero effects on attendance and bullying temper the broader case sometimes made for phone bans as a fix for those specific problems -- the study's own data does not support that expectation.

The scale of this study (nationwide GPS, test score, and survey data, staggered adoption timing) makes it one of the most methodologically rigorous evaluations of a widely adopted, low-nuance policy (blanket phone confiscation) rather than a small pilot study.
quotes: Phone restrictions in schools are spreading fast, but hard evidence has been thin. This US study evaluates one stringent version: lockable pouches (the Yondr brand) that students seal their phones into for the whole school day.

Using nationwide data on middle and high schools and a staggered difference-in-differences design, the researchers combined GPS phone signals, standardised test scores, attendance, discipline records and student surveys.
Adopting pouches sharply cut in-school phone use, with teachers reporting personal phone use in class falling from 61% to 13%.
Yet the wider effects were modest. Disciplinary incidents rose and student well-being dipped in the first year, then well-being turned positive and discipline settled.
Average test scores barely moved, with small gains in high school maths offset by small dips in middle schools. Attendance and bullying were unaffected.
